title: Defining Perfect Calibration
narration: Now let us make honest confidence precise. The paper defines perfect calibration with one equation, shown on the board. In words: among all predictions that come with confidence [[eq]]p, the fraction that are correct should equal p, for every p between zero and one. You asked where the paper says this: it is equation one in Section 2, Definitions. Let us work a tiny case. Take [[ten]]ten predictions, each with confidence zero point eight. A calibrated model should get eight of them right. Here are the ten, with eight marked correct and two wrong. The accuracy is eight out of ten, which is [[match]]zero point eight, matching the confidence. Now compare a second model with the same confidence of zero point eight, but only [[five]]five of the ten are correct. Its accuracy is zero point five, so it claims more than it delivers. That gap of zero point three is what we call [[over]]overconfidence. One practical note: confidence is a continuous number, so we cannot check this exactly with finite data. That is why the next step groups predictions into bins.

objects.tex: \mathbb{P}\big(\hat Y = Y \mid \hat P = p\big) = p,\quad \forall p \in [0,1]
